fun_highlights: The era/context system genuinely differentiates lives. War-era calling prompts ('There is a war on, and it is hungry for the young'), plague framings, and lean-year money pressure make the same structural beat read differently across dynasties. Returning player sees Dynasty 4 open with 'These are war years' and Dynasty 6 with 'a fever in the land' and the tone shift is immediate and real.

The observation pools are deep and calibrated by stat. The vit_tire pool alone has 18 distinct lines; the spirit_hi pool has 17. A returning player is unlikely to hit the same ambient texture line in back-to-back sessions. Engine comment '(jurors stopped reading it)' confirms the devs already fixed a previous staleness leak here.

The dynastic layer has genuine expressive power. The Okonkwo 5-generation arc (Dynasty 4) earns its motto 'We earn the bread we eat' and the heirloom 'a book too hard for a child's hands' creates a real through-line: it passes from Calla (age 7 origin) through Elias, Noor, Beatrix (who re-reads it at 47), to Hale. This is the genre working correctly — a lapsed player returning to that dynasty would feel real continuity.

Epitaph differentiation via RECENT_CLUSTERS and RECENT_LINES blocking is doing visible work. Across 15 dynasties the 'teacher' epitaph lands as 'Gave away everything she knew' (Selma, D9) and 'Poured what she knew into the young' (Ronja, D15) without literal repeats, and the theme-blocking prevents a single cluster from dominating a session.

Choice consequence bleeds forward in ways the player can trace. Calla strays at 44, speaks of it at 67, and decides it was right at 72 — three separate cards spanning 28 years all referencing the same act. This is the strongest argument for 'choices feel meaningful': the game remembers and returns.

The calling card genuinely branches into five shapes (soldier/scholar/maker/wanderer/adrift) and the adult/elder arc is vocation-gated enough that a wanderer's life (Hale, D4 gen 5: 'The road — go where the work is', midlife settling beat, late regret tally) reads structurally different from a scholar's (Henrik, D2; Otto, D7 gen3; Annika, D11 gen2).
staleness: The marriage prompt is the single most-seen card in the transcripts and its variance is insufficient for a lapsed player. Out of 15 dynasties, the 'Ask. Build a life.' resolution line fires in virtually every life that marries — and the

variants cluster visibly: D7gen5 Cleo ('Married Tobias, and the plain room felt larger'), D10gen2 Felix ('Married Lena. Nobody made a speech'), D13gen4 Mateo ('Married Matthias on an ordinary day, and meant every word of it'), D15gen4 Ronja ('Married Tomas after both had long stopped expecting it'). A returning player will immediately recognise the beat.

The childhood opening has six structural paths (era, seat, frailty, brightness, warmth, generic) but the generic pool of three lines is drawn almost every time for middle-of-the-road founders. Dynasty 1 Saoirse, Dynasty 5 Ottilie, Dynasty 6 Tomas, Dynasty 9 Selma, Dynasty 11 Ren all open with generic-pool variations. The player returns and sees 'Saoirse's earliest years pass the way most do' vs 'these are ordinary, half-remembered' — the pool is too small relative to how often it fires.

The 'masterwork deferred' beat (card not in the excerpt but its outcome appears verbatim in D6gen2 Cassian, D9gen2 Emory, D13gen2 Idris, D6gen4 Lucan who finally makes it): 'Kept the ordinary work coming and the lights on, and let the masterwork stay, as it always had, a thing he would make next year.' This four-word identical phrase ('a thing he would make next year') appears in three separate lives across two dynasties. The outcome line is not being varied.

The late-life body decline observation fires in almost every life past 55 and the phrasing, while drawn from a deep pool, produces recognisable rhythmic patterns — 'the body has begun sending its small bills', 'the weather has begun living in his joints', 'distances she once never thought about have started introducing themselves'. A lapsed player returning after weeks will hit this sequence in the first life they play and immediately recognise it as the template for the back half of every life.

The sickness card ('The sickness is in the next street, then the next house') fires across at least 7 of the 15 dynasties — Cassian Thorne, Vesna Thorne, Ingrid Thorne, Mira Thorne, Hale Okonkwo, Lucan Castellane, and both choices ('Tend them. Stay close.' / 'Keep your distance. Survive.') are presented identically each time with no era-aware framing. Dynasty 6 alone fires this card in three consecutive generations (Cassian at 35, Ingrid at 22, Mira at 48). The prompt text is single-variant and the player reads it verbatim three times.

The dying-wish 'what do you want remembered' card uses only three options across all lives: 'That I was kind.', 'That I built something.', 'That I was here at all.' This fires in D7gen2 Caleb, D10gen1 Tobias (chose built), D10gen2 Felix (chose built), D11gen2 Annika (chose kind), D12gen1 Mira (chose built), and the setup text 'A young one asks [Name] — who carried a blade — what he wants remembered. The question lands harder than expected' is invariant across all soldier-vocations. The whole card, from prompt to choice to outcome, reads as a template by the second or third time a returning player sees it.

improvements.what: Give the sickness card at least three prompt variants and gate one specifically to plague-era lives. Right now a single text ('The sickness is in the next street, then the next house. Someone close has it') fires verbatim across every life regardless of era, including non-plague ones.
improvements.why: It is the single most visually repeated prompt in the transcripts. Three consecutive Thorne generations see identical text. A simple freshPick on the prompt — and a separate, harsher text for plague-era lives — breaks the loudest repetition loop a lapsed player will hit.

improvements.what: Expand the 'masterwork deferred' outcome line. The phrase 'a thing he would make next year' appears verbatim at least three times across different characters. The outcome pool for this choice needs 5-6 variants, not one.
improvements.why: Outcome lines are less guarded than observation lines — they do not go through freshPick's session-memory system — so they repeat more visibly than ambient observations. A single repeated phrase in a choice outcome is the fastest way to feel like a template.

improvements.what: Add two or three framing variants to the 'what do you want remembered' card that are vocation-specific or era-specific. A soldier's version, a wanderer's version, a scholar's version. The current three generic options feel like a UI survey after a rich life.
improvements.why: This card fires late and is the last real moment of agency before death. Its thinness — three static options, one invariant prompt — undercuts an otherwise strong genre moment. It lands like a checkbox after a genuinely textured life.

improvements.what: Add a 'no-marriage' mid-life beat for lives where no love relation forms. Currently a life that never acquires 'love' simply skips a_marry silently. A deliberate 'the question never came' or 'chose the solitude' moment (even a brief non-choice observation at midlife) would make the absence feel authored rather than absent.
improvements.why: Several founders (Ren Holloway, Mira Halloran) reach midlife with no marriage and the transcript has a conspicuous gap where the a_marry beat would normally be. The game is otherwise good at narrating unchosen paths; this is a hole.

improvements.what: Introduce one or two dynastic callbacks that fire only for 3rd-generation-or-later heirs and reference a specific ancestor's action rather than just 'the family story'. The family-story card already exists (choosing to live up to or step out of a predecessor's shadow) but its text 'the one remembered, above all, for a fierce plain kindness' is generic. Wire it to actually name what the specific ancestor did — e.g. 'the one who built from ash' if their epitaph was the 'built' cluster.
improvements.why: The family-story card fires frequently in later generations (Beatrix D4gen4, Felix D10gen2, Mateo D13gen4, Ingrid D6gen4, Annika D11gen2) and its generic template text is immediately recognisable as a repeat. Making the callback specific to the actual ancestor's cluster would make each dynasty's later generations feel genuinely shaped by their particular history.

verdict: A Life has a strong foundation: the writing is clean and often genuinely good, the dynastic layer earns its keep in the longer playthroughs, and the choice-consequence callbacks (Calla's affair tracked across three late cards; the heirloom book passing through five hands) do what the genre promises. But as a lapsed player returning after weeks, I hit the template within two lives: the sickness prompt, the masterwork line, the marriage beat, the body-decline sequence all fire recognisably and the underlying structure becomes visible too quickly. The engine's anti-repeat machinery is working hard on observations but underprotects outcome lines and high-frequency interactive prompts. The game earns a second session but falters by the third; the enemy — staleness — is controlled, not defeated.
